findings.title: Keyword allow-list uses substring matching, so ordinary passphrase words slip through
findings.detail: onlyNames() decides a quoted value is "just a name" (and therefore not a leak) whenever it is camelCase or dash/underscore/dot-joined with no digits AND its lowercased form *contains* one of ["secret","token","password","passwd","key","client","vault","entry","access","name","id"]. Because this is a substring test rather than a per-word match, very common English words accidentally contain these tokens: "id" occurs in liquid/rapid/avoid/guide/wide/decide/provide/..., "key" occurs in monkey/turkey/donkey/whiskey/hockey, "name" occurs in surname/nickname/rename. A genuine diceware-style passphrase value such as `password = "mighty-river-liquid-stone"` or `apiKey = "whiskeyBarrelCanyon"` is all-lowercase/camelCase with no digits and contains "id"/"key" as a substring, so breaks()/onlyNames() will treat it as a mere "name for a secret" and silently drop the finding. This directly contradicts the change's stated guarantee that "weak passwords, passphrases and real keys still count": a real secret that happens to use a common dictionary word containing one of these substrings will no longer be flagged by the scanner, a regression in the security control the feature is supposed to strengthen. The existing test's passphrase example ("correct-horse-battery-staple") happens not to contain any of the listed substrings, so the test suite does not catch this.
